passage:
Lavanya's diary, Sunday night.
Went to my neighbour Minakshi's flat today. Her husband's funeral was on Friday, and the living room was full of relatives, all speaking in low voices and nobody sure what to do with their hands. I brought a pot of khichdi because I didn't know what else to bring. Minakshi's mother-in-law kept saying, “Just sit, beta.” So I sat. When one relative began a long story about a cousin's troubles, the room went stiff, and Minakshi's son stared at the wall. I washed the plates without asking. Later, at the door, Minakshi held my hand and said only, “Thank you for coming.” I had no perfect words, and it didn't seem to matter. I'll go on Thursday with lunch and stay an hour.
Lavanya

qa.q: What did Lavanya bring to Minakshi's flat?
qa.a: Lavanya brought a pot of khichdi.

qa.q: What did Lavanya feel about not having perfect words?
qa.a: Lavanya felt unsure and a little helpless at first, and then seemed to be reassured, since Minakshi only said “Thank you for coming” and the missing words did not seem to matter.

qa.q: What did Lavanya choose to do in the room that helped?
qa.a: Lavanya sat when told to, washed the plates without being asked and planned another visit with lunch, offering presence and small practical help, not speeches.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Minakshi's son when the relative told the long story?
qa.a: Minakshi's son may have felt uncomfortable or numb, since the room went stiff and he stared at the wall, and a long story may have made his own loss harder to bear. 🤍

grounding: An adult brings food, shows up, listens and does small practical tasks for a bereaved family, since presence is worth more than perfect words.

passage: I'm Nandini, and I live next door to Bidisha. I was at her fifth birthday. passage: “We had a club when I was ten,” said Mausi Manjula. “The Seven Stars. We met behind the water tank in our colony. To join, you hopped on one leg round the tank and swore on a paper star. Our leader, Pinky, said a proper club needed exactly seven, so no eighth member. Then Gurpreet moved into the flat above ours. He was so eager! He hopped so well round the tank. But Pinky said, ‘Seven only.’ I remember Gurpreet's face. After that, the rest of us made our own rule: anyone could hop.” She laughed. “We dropped the number and called ourselves The Stars.”

qa.a: Gurpreet was probably hurt and disappointed, since Gurpreet had hopped so well and was still turned away.

qa.q: What was the turning point that changed the club?
qa.a: The rest of the children decided that anyone could hop, and dropped the number, so the club no longer left newcomers out.

qa.a: Pinky may have wanted the club to feel special and firm, and did not see how much the fixed number would hurt someone new.

grounding: Children invent a club with a ritual that marks who belongs, and an elder recalls how it left someone out.

passage: The rain hammered the roof while the whole family crowded into the small room for the annual remembrance ritual. passage: Every Sunday evening, Neelam's family lit a lamp in the flat and said the same prayer together before dinner. Neelam had never questioned it before. Tonight, as Papa struck the match, the words felt unfamiliar in the mouth. Neelam stayed silent while the others chanted, then noticed that Seema, Neelam's mother, had noticed. At the table Seema asked quietly, “You weren't saying it. What's going on?” Neelam's heart thumped. “I love the lamp part. But I don't know if I believe the words, and I don't want to fake it.” Seema paused, then passed the rice. “Tell me more. I'd like to hear what you think.” Papa cleared his throat but said nothing.

qa.q: What did Neelam's family do every Sunday evening?

qa.a: Neelam seems unsure whether the words are believed and does not want to say them without meaning it.

qa.q: What choice did Neelam make at the table, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Neelam answered honestly and respectfully, loving the lamp but unsure of the words, and Seema invited more, so the question became a conversation.

qa.q: What might Papa have been feeling when Papa cleared his throat but said nothing?
qa.a: Papa may have felt uneasy or unsure how to respond, though Papa let Seema lead the conversation.

grounding: A teenager wonders whether they believe an inherited ritual, feels tension between love for family and wanting to own beliefs, and asks respectfully.

passage: The school theatre club had a tradition: on show day everyone wore black and, before the curtain, mocked the rival drama group with a short parody. Trisha loved the club. Twelve people, one captain, Jomon, and the best hours of her week. This year she stood in the circle as the parody script was passed round. Everyone laughed. She stayed silent, then spoke. “I'll wear black and paint the sets, but I'd rather not do the parody.” Jomon raised an eyebrow. “It's tradition.” “I know. I still want to be here.” A boy shrugged. Two others nodded. Jomon paused, then said, “Fine. Sets and lights, then.” Trisha exhaled.

qa.a: Trisha offered to wear black and paint the sets but said she would rather not do the parody, and added that she still wanted to be there.

qa.q: How might Jomon have seen Trisha's refusal?
qa.a: Jomon probably felt challenged by a break in tradition but wanted to keep Trisha in the club, which fits the pause and the offer of sets and lights.

passage: On the third night, the seniors gathered the first-years in the hostel common room. “Belong first, belong properly,” one said. Each fresher was told to stand on a chair and announce that they were useless, then carry a senior's bag around the block. Most did it, laughing tightly. Nikita went along, eyes on the floor. Devika stepped forward when her turn came and said, “I'll introduce myself, but I won't do that.” The room went quiet. One senior sneered. Devika walked out with her heart pounding. passage:
Dear Pooja,
You asked why I sounded odd on the phone. Here it is. The rowing club's welcome week was supposed to be fun. On the first night the seniors made us stand in the hall and shout that we were nobodies. On the second we carried their bags and sang in the dining hall while they filmed. On the third they wanted us to do a dare I knew was unsafe. I wanted so badly to belong that I nearly did. Instead I said no and walked out. On Friday I went to the faculty adviser. She listened, said it wasn't my fault, and called both captains in that same afternoon. I'm still shaky, and a few first-years won't talk to me. But two of them came to my room yesterday.
Asif

qa.a: The seniors made them stand in the hall and shout that they were nobodies.

Daniel grinned. “Teach me.” The following Sunday, five students crowded round two burners, and Tuan ladled the first bowl, closed his eyes for a second and smiled.

passage: Every morning at home, Sudha woke to filter coffee and her mother's humming from the kitchen. In the university hostel, the alarm rang in a corridor of closed doors. passage: Every year on the last working day of December, the factory floor stopped for ten minutes. The whole shift gathered by the loading bay, where Francis, the sixty-year-old night guard, led a short prayer of thanks. Kiran, in the second row, wasn't a believer and felt awkward, but stood with head bowed. Around Kiran most people closed their eyes; two supervisors looked at their watches; a young technician whispered a joke and stopped when nobody laughed. When Francis's voice cracked at the name of a colleague who had died in the spring, Kiran opened both eyes and saw Francis wiping tears with the back of a hand. Afterwards Kiran didn't pretend to have prayed. “Thank you for doing that,” Kiran said. Francis nodded and gave Kiran a piece of cake.

qa.q: How long did the factory floor stop for the prayer?
qa.a: The factory floor stopped for ten minutes.

qa.a: Kiran felt awkward, since Kiran was not a believer, but still wanted to be respectful.
